title: Hiragana and Katakana
intro: Hiragana and katakana are two ways of writing the same 46 sounds. Every hiragana has a katakana twin that says exactly the same thing, so this page teaches them as pairs: each row shows the hiragana and katakana side by side, with tips for both. Learn one sound and you get two shapes. Hiragana is for Japanese words, word endings and small grammar words like wa, no and desu. Katakana is for words borrowed from other languages, foreign names, sound effects and emphasis.

sections.title: Lessons
sections.html:
How to learn them as pairs

Take one row at a time. Say the sound, write the hiragana, then write the katakana next to it. Hiragana is round and flowing, and katakana is short, straight and angular, but several pairs look almost the same, such as か and カ, き and キ, せ and セ, へ and ヘ, も and モ, and り and リ. Start with those, because you learn two shapes for the price of one.

The marks work the same way in both scripts. Two dashes make a voiced sound (か becomes が, カ becomes ガ), a small circle makes a p sound (は becomes ぱ, ハ becomes パ), and a small や, ゆ or よ (ャ, ュ or ョ) blends into one beat. The two scripts differ in only a few places: katakana writes long vowels with a dash (ー), has extra sounds for foreign words like ティ and ファ, and is never used for particles.

Vowels (a i u e o)

RomajiHiraganaKatakanaHiragana exampleKatakana example
aあアあめ (ame), rainアメリカ (amerika), America
iいイいす (isu), chairイギリス (igirisu), United Kingdom
uうウうち (uchi), house, homeウール (u-ru), wool
eえエえき (eki), train stationエンジニア (enjinia), engineer
oおオおかね (okane), moneyオフィス (ofisu), office

Hiragana

These five sounds are the base of every other row, so learn them first. Each vowel is short and clean. Say a as in father, i as in see, u as in food (with relaxed lips), e as in pet and o as in more, but shorter. Keep your mouth still while you say each one, so it does not glide into a second sound the way English oh and ay do.

Memory hooks: あ is an apple with a stem. い is two eels side by side. う is a small hat on a tilted U. え is an exotic bird with a long tail. お is a person with a round belly shouting oh.

Write each one by hand three times while you say it out loud. Your fingers remember shapes that your eyes forget.

Katakana

Katakana uses the same five vowel sounds as hiragana: a as in father, i as in see, u as in food (with relaxed lips), e as in pet and o as in more, but shorter. Only the shapes are new. Katakana strokes are short, straight and angular, and many of them are parts of kanji.

Memory hooks: ア is the axe that splits the apple. イ is a tall eel leaning on a pole. ウ is う with a bigger hat on straight sides. エ is an I-beam, like the shaft of an elevator (エレベーター). オ is お with the belly cut off.

Write each one by hand three times while you say it out loud. Start and stop each stroke clearly, because katakana looks sloppy when the lines are curved.

K row (ka ki ku ke ko)

RomajiHiraganaKatakanaHiragana exampleKatakana example
kaかカかさ (kasa), umbrellaカメラ (kamera), camera
kiきキきた (kita), northキロ (kiro), kilometer, kilogram
kuくクくち (kuchi), mouthクラス (kurasu), class
keけケけさ (kesa), this morningケーキ (ke-ki), cake
koこコこども (kodomo), childコーヒー (ko-hi-), coffee

Hiragana

Add a k sound in front of each vowel. Keep the k light, with less puff of air than in English. This row is also the first one that can take two small dashes to make the g sounds, which you meet later in this file.

Memory hooks: か is a karate chop with a small flick. き is a key with teeth. く is a cuckoo's open beak. け is a keg of beer with a tap on its side. こ is two koi fish, one above the other.

Katakana

Memory hooks: カ is か with the chop straightened, and it looks like the kanji 力. キ is a key drawn with straight lines. ク is a cuckoo's beak. ケ is a keg tipped over. コ is a corner, squeezing the koi fish into a box.

S row (sa shi su se so)

RomajiHiraganaKatakanaHiragana exampleKatakana example
saさサさかな (sakana), fishサラダ (sarada), salad
shiしシしごと (shigoto), work, jobシンガポール (shingapo-ru), Singapore
suすスすし (sushi), sushiスプーン (supu-n), spoon
seせセせんせい (sensei), teacherセーター (se-ta-), sweater
soそソそと (soto), outsideソフトウェア (sofutowea), software

Hiragana

One spelling breaks the pattern: し is shi, not si. It sounds like the English word she. The u in す is often very quiet at the end of a word, as in です, which you meet in the silent vowels lesson.

Memory hooks: さ is a samurai holding a sword. し is a fishing hook. す is a piece of sushi with a curl of rice. せ is a seesaw with a long plank. そ is a zigzag of sewing thread.

Katakana

One spelling breaks the pattern: シ is shi, not si, and it sounds like the English word she. Be careful, because シ looks a lot like ツ and ソ looks a lot like ン. The Easy to mix up section shows how to tell them apart.

Memory hooks: サ is a samurai with a straight sword. シ has two dots lying down like eyes and a smile sweeping up. She smiles. ス is a super hero's cape blowing in the wind. セ is the seesaw plank with straight edges. ソ is a sewing needle with a dot above and a long slanted stroke.

T row (ta chi tsu te to)

RomajiHiraganaKatakanaHiragana exampleKatakana example
taたタたまご (tamago), eggタクシー (takushi-), taxi
chiちチちかく (chikaku), nearbyチーズ (chi-zu), cheese
tsuつツつくえ (tsukue), deskツアー (tsua-), tour
teてテてがみ (tegami), letterテレビ (terebi), television
toとトとけい (tokei), clock, watchトイレ (toire), toilet

Hiragana

Two sounds break the pattern: ち is chi and つ is tsu. For tsu, put the tip of your tongue just behind your top teeth, say the ts at the end of the English word cats, then add u. Do not say tu or su.

Memory hooks: た is the letters t and a squeezed together. ち looks like a 5, so picture five slices of cheese. つ is a tsunami wave curling over. て is an open hand, and the kanji for hand, 手, is read te. と is a toe with a thorn stuck in it.

Katakana

Memory hooks: タ is a table (ta-ble) with a slanted leg, and it looks like the kanji 夕. チ looks like the kanji 千, the number thousand. ツ is three splashes of spray flying up from a tsunami. テ is a TV antenna, and it starts テレビ. ト is a totem pole with one arm out.

N row (na ni nu ne no)

RomajiHiraganaKatakanaHiragana exampleKatakana example
naなナなまえ (namae), nameナイフ (naifu), knife
niにニにほん (nihon), Japanアニメ (anime), animation, anime
nuぬヌいぬ (inu), dogヌードル (nu-doru), noodles
neねネねこ (neko), catネクタイ (nekutai), necktie
noのノのり (nori), seaweedノート (no-to), notebook

Hiragana

This is an n sound in front of each vowel. Do not mix the whole row up with ん, the single n kana at the end of the chart. Two characters here, ぬ and ね, are easy to confuse with め and れ, so read the Easy to mix up section when you are ready.

Memory hooks: な is a nun kneeling in prayer. に looks like 二, the number two, which is read ni. ぬ is a noodle wound around a chopstick. ね is a cat (neko) with a curled tail. の is a circle with a swish, like a sign saying no.

Katakana

Memory hooks: ナ is just the nun's cross. ニ is two lines, like the kanji 二, which is read ni. ヌ is a noodle pinched into a sharp bend. ネ is the knot of a necktie, and it starts ネクタイ. ノ is a single slash, like the line through a no-entry sign.

H row (ha hi fu he ho)

RomajiHiraganaKatakanaHiragana exampleKatakana example
haはハはる (haru), springハードウェア (ha-dowea), hardware
hiひヒひと (hito), personヒーター (hi-ta-), heater
fuふフふゆ (fuyu), winterフランス (furansu), France
heへヘへや (heya), roomヘリコプター (herikoputa-), helicopter
hoほホほん (hon), bookホテル (hoteru), hotel

Hiragana

ふ is fu, made by blowing softly between your lips, somewhere between English f and h. は and へ change their sound when they work as grammar words: は is read wa and へ is read e. You practise that in the particles lesson.

Memory hooks: は is a person laughing out loud, ha ha. ひ is a wide grin, hee hee. ふ is Mount Fuji with a patch of cloud. へ is a hill: hey, a hill! ほ is は with an extra bar, like Santa laughing ho ho ho.

Katakana

フ is fu, made by blowing softly between your lips, somewhere between English f and h. Katakana has no particles, so ハ and ヘ always keep the sounds ha and he.

Memory hooks: ハ is a hat with two sloping sides, and it looks like the kanji 八. ヒ is a heel, the side view of a bent foot. フ is a flag hanging from a pole. ヘ is a hill, the twin of へ. ホ is a Christmas tree.

M row (ma mi mu me mo)

RomajiHiraganaKatakanaHiragana exampleKatakana example
maまマまど (mado), windowマニラ (manira), Manila
miみミみみ (mimi), earミルク (miruku), milk
muむムむし (mushi), insect, bugゲーム (ge-mu), game
meめメめがね (megane), eyeglassesメモ (memo), memo
moもモもも (momo), peachモール (mo-ru), mall

Hiragana

This is a plain m sound in front of each vowel, so the row has no surprises for your ears. For your eyes, ま, み and む all have loops, so compare their shapes slowly.

Memory hooks: ま is a mama with her arms out and a bundle at her feet. み is a number 3 with a tail, and mittsu means three. む is a cow saying moo, with a small horn on the right. め is an eye, and the kanji for eye, 目, is read me. も is a fish hook with two worms, and you want mo(re) worms.

Katakana

This is a plain m sound in front of each vowel. Look closely at the shapes: ミ is three lines, ム is a pointed snout and メ is an X.

Memory hooks: マ is a mallet with a flat head and a slanted handle. ミ is three slanted lines, like the number 3, and mittsu means three. ム is the cow's pointed snout and horn. メ is an X, and X marks me. モ is a fish hook straightened out, with two worms.

Y row (ya yu yo)

RomajiHiraganaKatakanaHiragana exampleKatakana example
yaやヤやすみ (yasumi), holiday, day offタイヤ (taiya), tire
yuゆユゆき (yuki), snowユニフォーム (yunifo-mu), uniform
yoよヨよる (yoru), nightヨーロッパ (yo-roppa), Europe

Hiragana

This row has only three characters. The basic chart has no yi or ye. The same three shapes, written smaller, are used in combination sounds like きゃ, so learn them well now.

Memory hooks: や is a yak with a long horn on top. ゆ is a fish swimming in a hot spring, and yu means hot water. よ is a yo-yo on its string.

Katakana

Memory hooks: ヤ is a yacht with a tall mast and a slanted sail. ユ is a U-shaped pool, and yu means hot water. ヨ is a backwards E with three bars.

R row (ra ri ru re ro)

RomajiHiraganaKatakanaHiragana exampleKatakana example
raらラらいげつ (raigetsu), next monthラーメン (ra-men), ramen
riりリりんご (ringo), appleリゾート (rizo-to), resort
ruるルくるま (kuruma), carルール (ru-ru), rule
reれレれいぞうこ (reizouko), refrigeratorレストラン (resutoran), restaurant
roろロろく (roku), sixロビー (robi-), lobby

Hiragana

The Japanese r is a very quick tap of the tongue just behind your top teeth. It sits between English r, l and d, so do not roll it and do not pull your tongue back. Two pairs look alike, る and ろ, and れ and ね, so study them with care.

Memory hooks: ら is a rabbit sitting with one ear up. り is two reeds by a river bank. る is a road that ends in a small loop. れ is ね with the loop taken out, so it has been re-moved. ろ is a plain road (ro-ad) with no loop.

Katakana

Memory hooks: ラ is the rabbit seen from behind. リ is two reeds, shorter and straighter than り. ル is two legs running (ru-n). レ is a check mark, the kind you make when you re-check (re) your work. ロ is a box, a room (ro-om), and it looks like the kanji 口.

W row (wa wo)

RomajiHiraganaKatakanaHiragana exampleKatakana example
waわワわたし (watashi), Iワイン (wain), wine
oをヲごはんを たべます (gohan o tabemasu), I eat a meal.ヲタク (otaku), a fan, an enthusiast

Hiragana

わ is wa. を is pronounced o, exactly like お. In modern Japanese you use it only as a particle that marks what a verb acts on, so you will almost never see it inside a word. In romaji it is written o, though some systems write wo.

Memory hooks: わ is someone shouting wa! in surprise. を is an acrobat in mid-air shouting woah.

Katakana

ワ is wa. ヲ is pronounced o, like オ, but it is very rare, because katakana has no particle that needs it. You will find it mostly in the spelling ヲタク and in old or stylized writing. Spend your time on ワ.

Memory hooks: ワ is ウ without its hat, a water (wa-ter) glass with no lid. ヲ is the acrobat drawn with straight lines, and it is very rare.

N (n)

RomajiHiraganaKatakanaHiragana exampleKatakana example
nんンほん (hon), bookラーメン (ra-men), ramen
nんンしんぶん (shinbun), newspaper, where n sounds like mコンピューター (konpyu-ta-), computer, where n sounds like m
nんンてんき (tenki), weather, where n sounds like ngハンバーガー (hanba-ga-), hamburger, where n sounds like m
nんンきんえん (kin'en), no smoking, with an apostrophe in romajiオンエア (on'ea), on air, with an apostrophe in romaji
nんンほんや (hon'ya), bookstore, with an apostrophe in romaji

Hiragana

ん is the only kana that is a consonant with no vowel. It is a full beat on its own, so こんにちは has five beats: ko, n, ni, chi, wa. No word begins with ん. You always write ん, but your mouth changes a little around it: before b, m or p it sounds like m, and before k or g it sounds like ng, which your Chapter 1 phonetics page shows with shinbun and tenki.

When ん comes before a vowel or a y sound, romaji adds an apostrophe so you can see the break. Compare kin'en (no smoking) with kinen (anniversary).

Memory hooks: ん is a cursive lowercase n.

Katakana

ン is the only kana that is a consonant with no vowel, and it is a full beat on its own. No word begins with ン. Before b, m or p it sounds like m, and before k or g it sounds like ng, but you always write ン. When ン comes before a vowel, romaji adds an apostrophe so you can see the break.

Do not mix ン up with ソ. ン starts low and sweeps up, while ソ starts at the top and falls.

Memory hooks: ン is a short stroke and a long stroke that sweeps up, like an n heading uphill.

G row (ga gi gu ge go)

RomajiHiraganaKatakanaHiragana exampleKatakana example
gaがガがくせい (gakusei), studentガソリン (gasorin), gasoline
giぎギぎんこう (ginkou), bankギター (gita-), guitar
guぐグぐらい (gurai), about, approximatelyグループ (guru-pu), group
geげゲげんき (genki), healthy, wellゲスト (gesuto), guest
goごゴごはん (gohan), meal, cooked riceゴルフ (gorufu), golf

Hiragana

Two small dashes, called dakuten (or ten-ten), turn a k sound into a g sound. The mouth shape stays the same, but your throat hums. Put your fingers on your throat to feel it. Some speakers soften g to ng in the middle of a word, so arigatou can sound like aringatou. Both are fine.

The dakuten is only a mark. If you can read か, you can already read が.

Katakana

Two small dashes, called dakuten (or ten-ten), turn a k sound into a g sound. They work exactly as in hiragana: say the plain sound, hum it, and you have the marked one.

Z row (za ji zu ze zo)

RomajiHiraganaKatakanaHiragana exampleKatakana example
zaざザざっし (zasshi), magazineピザ (piza), pizza
jiじジじかん (jikan), timeページ (pe-ji), page
zuずズちず (chizu), mapズボン (zubon), trousers
zeぜゼぜんぶ (zenbu), all, the whole thingゼロ (zero), zero
zoぞゾかぞく (kazoku), familyゾーン (zo-n), zone

Hiragana

Dakuten on the s row gives the z row. One sound changes spelling: じ is ji, as in jeep, not zi. The marks work the same way for every row: say the plain sound, hum it, and you have the marked one.

Katakana

Dakuten on the s row gives the z row. ジ is ji, as in jeep, not zi. Loanwords use this row for the English j, as in ジュース (juice), and for the English z, as in ゼロ (zero).

D row (da ji zu de do)

RomajiHiraganaKatakanaHiragana exampleKatakana example
daだダだいがく (daigaku), universityダンス (dansu), dance
jiぢヂはなぢ (hanaji), nosebleed
zuづヅつづく (tsuzuku), to continue
deでデでんわ (denwa), telephoneデパート (depa-to), department store
doどドどうぞ (douzo), please, go aheadドイツ (doitsu), Germany

Hiragana

Dakuten on the t row gives だ, で and ど, which are regular. ぢ and づ also exist, but they sound exactly like じ and ず, and they appear in only a few words, usually when ち or つ becomes voiced inside a word. When you write ji or zu yourself, use じ and ず.

Katakana

Dakuten on the t row gives ダ, デ and ド, which are regular. ヂ and ヅ also exist, but they sound exactly like ジ and ズ, and they are almost never used in katakana, so they have no katakana example word here. When you write ji or zu, use ジ and ズ.

B row (ba bi bu be bo)

RomajiHiraganaKatakanaHiragana exampleKatakana example
baばバばんごう (bangou), numberバス (basu), bus
biびビびじゅつ (bijutsu), artビル (biru), building
buぶブぶちょう (buchou), department headブーツ (bu-tsu), boots
beべベべんきょう (benkyou), studyベッド (beddo), bed
boぼボぼうし (boushi), hatボールペン (bo-rupen), ballpoint pen

Hiragana

Dakuten on the h row gives the b row. Close your lips for the b, then open them for the vowel. Notice that the same h row also gives a p row with a different mark, which comes next.

Katakana

P row (pa pi pu pe po)

RomajiHiraganaKatakanaHiragana exampleKatakana example
paぱパかんぱい (kanpai), cheers, a toastパン (pan), bread
piぴピえんぴつ (enpitsu), pencilピアノ (piano), piano
puぷプてんぷら (tenpura), tempuraプレゼント (purezento), present, gift
peぺペぺらぺら (perapera), fluent (in a language)ペン (pen), pen
poぽポさんぽ (sanpo), a walk, a strollポスト (posuto), mailbox

Hiragana

A small circle, called handakuten, turns an h sound into a p sound. It is used only on the h row, so there are exactly five of these kana. Be careful: two dashes make b and a small circle makes p, so は becomes ば or ぱ.

Katakana

Combination sounds: K and G (kya kyu kyo gya gyu gyo)

RomajiHiraganaKatakanaHiragana exampleKatakana example
kyaきゃキャきゃく (kyaku), guest, customerキャベツ (kyabetsu), cabbage
kyuきゅキュきゅうり (kyuuri), cucumberキュート (kyu-to), cute
kyoきょキョきょう (kyou), todayキョロキョロ (kyorokyoro), looking around restlessly
gyaぎゃギャぎゃく (gyaku), opposite, reverseギャラリー (gyarari-), gallery
gyuぎゅギュぎゅうにゅう (gyuunyuu), milkギュッと (gyutto), tightly, with a squeeze
gyoぎょギョぎょうざ (gyouza), fried dumplingsギョーザ (gyo-za), fried dumplings

Hiragana

A combination sound, which your Chapter 1 phonetics page calls a contracted sound, joins a kana that ends in i with a small や, ゆ or よ. The two kana make one beat. Write the small kana smaller, low on the line and close to the kana before it. So きゃ is kya, one beat, while き followed by a full-size や is ki-ya, two beats.

The pattern is easy: take the i kana, drop the i, and add ya, yu or yo. き (ki) becomes kya, kyu and kyo.

Katakana

Combination sounds: S and J (sha shu sho ja ju jo)

RomajiHiraganaKatakanaHiragana exampleKatakana example
shaしゃシャしゃいん (shain), company employeeシャツ (shatsu), shirt
shuしゅシュしゅくだい (shukudai), homeworkシュート (shu-to), a shot (in sports)
shoしょショしょくじ (shokuji), mealショッピング (shoppingu), shopping
jaじゃジャじゃがいも (jagaimo), potatoジャム (jamu), jam
juじゅジュじゅうじ (juuji), ten o'clockジュース (ju-su), juice
joじょジョじょうず (jouzu), good at, skilledジョギング (jogingu), jogging

Hiragana

Both of these groups spell differently from the usual pattern. し plus a small や is sha, not shya, and じ plus a small や is ja, not jya. The same goes for shu, sho, ju and jo.

Katakana

Combination sounds: CH and NY (cha chu cho nya nyu nyo)

RomajiHiraganaKatakanaHiragana exampleKatakana example
chaちゃチャちゃわん (chawan), rice bowlチャンス (chansu), chance
chuちゅチュちゅうしゃじょう (chuushajou), parking lotチューリップ (chu-rippu), tulip
choちょチョちょっと (chotto), a little, a momentチョコレート (chokore-to), chocolate
nyaにゃニャこんにゃく (konnyaku), konjac, a jelly-like foodニャー (nya-), meow
nyuにゅニュにゅういん (nyuuin), staying in the hospitalニュース (nyu-su), news
nyoにょニョにょうぼう (nyoubou), wife (old-fashioned)ニョッキ (nyokki), gnocchi

Hiragana

ち plus a small や is cha, not chya. The same goes for chu and cho. The ny sounds sound like the ny in canyon: に plus a small や is nya.

The kana みゅ (myu) and ぴゅ (pyu) exist, but they are so rare that no everyday word uses them, so they have no hiragana example word in these tables.

Katakana

Combination sounds: H, B and P (hya hyu hyo bya byu byo pya pyo)

RomajiHiraganaKatakanaHiragana exampleKatakana example
hyaひゃヒャひゃく (hyaku), one hundred
hyuひゅヒュひゅうひゅう (hyuuhyuu), whistling of the windヒューマン (hyu-man), human
hyoひょヒョひょう (hyou), chart, tableヒョウ (hyou), leopard
byaびゃビャさんびゃく (sanbyaku), three hundred
byuびゅビュびゅうびゅう (byuubyuu), howling of the windビュッフェ (byuffe), buffet
byoびょビョびょうき (byouki), illness, sicknessビョーク (byo-ku), Bjork (a singer)
pyaぴゃピャはっぴゃく (happyaku), eight hundred
pyoぴょピョぴょんぴょん (pyonpyon), hopping up and downピョンピョン (pyonpyon), hopping up and down
pyuぴゅピュピューマ (pyu-ma), puma

Hiragana

Here the h, b and p rows blend with a small や, ゆ or よ. You will see ひゃく (100) and びょうき (illness) most often. These combinations also show up in number words: さんびゃく (300) uses bya, and はっぴゃく (800) uses a small っ and pya.

Katakana

The h, b and p rows blend with a small ユ or ヨ in a handful of loanwords. The combinations ヒャ (hya), ビャ (bya) and ピャ (pya) exist too, but they are so rare in katakana that they have no katakana example word here.

Combination sounds: M and R (mya myu myo rya ryu ryo)

RomajiHiraganaKatakanaHiragana exampleKatakana example
myaみゃミャみゃく (myaku), pulseミャンマー (myanma-), Myanmar
myoみょミョみょうにち (myounichi), tomorrow (formal)ミョウガ (myouga), Japanese ginger
ryaりゃリャりゃく (ryaku), abbreviationリャマ (ryama), llama
ryuりゅリュりゅうがくせい (ryuugakusei), international studentリュック (ryukku), backpack
ryoりょリョりょこう (ryokou), travel, a tripリョウタ (ryouta), Ryota (a boy's name)
myuみゅミュミュージック (myu-jikku), music

Hiragana

The same rule works for m and r: み plus a small や is mya, and り plus a small よ is ryo. The most useful ones are りょ, りゅ and みょ. The kana みゅ (myu) exists but no everyday word uses it.

Katakana

The same rule works for m and r: ミ plus a small ヤ is mya, and リ plus a small ユ is ryu. Words like ミュージック (music) and リュック (backpack) are the ones you will meet most often.

Small tsu (っ and ッ)

Hiragana

A small っ makes no sound of its own. It marks a very short pause that doubles the next consonant. In romaji you double that consonant, so がっこう is gakkou, きって is kitte and ざっし is zasshi. Before ch, romaji uses tch, as in まっちゃ (matcha). A small っ always sits in the middle of a word and always counts as one full beat.

Say it like the pause in the English phrase hot tea, where you hold the t for an extra moment.

KanaRomajiExample wordMeaning
っこkkoがっこう (gakkou)school
っとttoちょっと (chotto)a little, a moment
っぷppuきっぷ (kippu)ticket
っしsshiざっし (zasshi)magazine
っぱppaすっぱい (suppai)sour
っつttsuみっつ (mittsu)three things
っちゃtchaまっちゃ (matcha)powdered green tea

Katakana

A small ッ makes no sound of its own. It marks a very short pause that doubles the next consonant. In romaji you double that consonant, so サッカー is sakka-, ベッド is beddo and カップ is kappu. Before ch, romaji uses tch, as in キッチン (kitchin). A small ッ usually sits in the middle of a word and always counts as one full beat.

Loanwords use ッ a lot, because English words often end in a hard consonant, like cup, bed and bag. Japanese adds a small ッ and a vowel to copy that sound.

KanaRomajiExample wordMeaning
ッカkkaサッカー (sakka-)soccer
ッドddoベッド (beddo)bed
ッグgguバッグ (baggu)bag
ップppuカップ (kappu)cup
ッチtchiキッチン (kitchin)kitchen
ッシュsshuダッシュ (dasshu)a dash, a sprint
ットttoホット (hotto)hot

Long vowels (hiragana vowels and the katakana ー)

Hiragana

A long vowel lasts twice as long as a short one, and the length can change the word. In hiragana you add a vowel kana: あ after an a kana, い after an i kana, う after a u kana, え after an e kana, and お after an o kana.

Two spellings need special care. A long e is written with え in a few words, such as おねえさん, but most words use い, as in せんせい (sensei, said like sensee). A long o is usually written with う, as in こうこう (koukou, said like kookoo), but a few words use お, as in おおきい (ookii). Romaji copies the kana, so you see ei and ou.

KanaRomajiExample wordMeaning
かあkaaおかあさん (okaasan)mother
にいniiおにいさん (oniisan)older brother
くうkuuくうこう (kuukou)airport
ねえneeおねえさん (oneesan)older sister
せいseiせんせい (sensei)teacher
おおooおおきい (ookii)big
こうkouこうこう (koukou)high school
とうtouありがとう (arigatou)thank you

Katakana

Katakana does not add a vowel kana to make a long vowel. It uses a dash called ー instead, which means hold the vowel before it for twice as long. In romaji it is written as a hyphen, so コーヒー is ko-hi-. In horizontal text the dash lies flat, and in vertical text it stands upright.

The dash matters, because length changes the word: ビル (biru) is a building and ビール (bi-ru) is beer.

KanaRomajiExample wordMeaning
アーa-カード (ka-do)card
イーi-ビール (bi-ru)beer
ウーu-スープ (su-pu)soup
エーe-ケーキ (ke-ki)cake
オーo-ノート (no-to)notebook
ヒーhi-コーヒー (ko-hi-)coffee

Particles は, へ and を (wa, e, o)

Three hiragana change their sound when they work as particles, the small grammar words that attach to other words. は is read wa, へ is read e and を is read o. Everywhere else they keep their usual sounds, so はる is haru and へや is heya.

The greetings こんにちは and こんばんは end in は read wa for the same historical reason.

KanaRomajiExample wordMeaning
はwaわたしは がくせいです。 (watashi wa gakusei desu.)I am a student.
はwaこんにちは (konnichiwa)hello, good day
はwaこんばんは (konbanwa)good evening
へeがっこうへ いきます。 (gakkou e ikimasu.)I go to school.
をoみずを のみます。 (mizu o nomimasu.)I drink water.

Silent vowels (desu and masu)

In everyday speech, i and u often almost disappear between quiet consonants. です sounds like dess, ます sounds like mass, and the first し in しつれいします is barely heard. Your Chapter 1 phonetics page calls this a devocalized sound. You still write every kana, and you do not need to leave the vowel out when you speak slowly.

KanaRomajiExample wordMeaning
すsuわたしは がくせいです。 (watashi wa gakusei desu.)I am a student. (desu sounds like dess)
すsuききます (kikimasu)to listen (sounds like kikimass)
くkuりゅうがくせい (ryuugakusei)international student (the ku is quiet)
すsuわかっています (wakatteimasu)I understand (the su is quiet)
しshiしつれいします (shitsureishimasu)excuse me (the first shi is quiet)

Extra sounds with F, katakana only (fa fi fe fo)

Katakana has extra combinations for sounds that native Japanese words do not have. A small vowel (ァ ィ ェ ォ) after a full-size kana blends with it into one beat. The big kana gives the consonant and the small vowel gives the vowel. フ plus a small ア is fa.

The Japanese f is soft. Blow gently between your lips instead of pressing your top teeth on your bottom lip.

KanaRomajiExample wordMeaning
ファfaファイル (fairu)file
フィfiフィリピン (firipin)Philippines
フェfeカフェ (kafe)cafe
フォfoフォーク (fo-ku)fork

Extra sounds with T and D, katakana only (ti di)

テ plus a small ィ is ti, and デ plus a small ィ is di. Native Japanese words have no ti or di, so these combinations were added for foreign words. Two rarer sounds follow the same rule: トゥ is tu and ドゥ is du.

Read ティ as one beat. It is not te-i.

KanaRomajiExample wordMeaning
ティtiパーティー (pa-ti-)party
ディdiディナー (dina-)dinner

Extra sounds with W, katakana only (wi we wo)

ウ plus a small ィ, ェ or ォ gives wi, we and wo. Note that ウォーター is wo-ta-, not uo-ta-, because the small kana blends with ウ into one beat.

KanaRomajiExample wordMeaning
ウィwiウィスキー (wisuki-)whisky
ウェweウェブ (webu)web
ウォwoウォーター (wo-ta-)water

Extra sounds with V, katakana only (va vi ve vo)

ヴ is ウ with two dots, and it stands for the English v. With a small ァ, ィ, ェ or ォ it gives va, vi, ve and vo. Many words use バ, ビ, ブ, ベ and ボ instead, so you may see both spellings, such as ヴァイオリン and バイオリン for violin. The plain ヴ (vu) is rare.

KanaRomajiExample wordMeaning
ヴァvaヴァイオリン (vaiorin)violin
ヴィviヴィーナス (vi-nasu)Venus
ヴェveヴェール (ve-ru)veil
ヴォvoヴォーカル (vo-karu)vocal

Extra sounds with SH, J and CH, katakana only (she je che)

シ, ジ and チ plus a small ェ give she, je and che. They copy English words like share, jet and check.

KanaRomajiExample wordMeaning
シェsheシェア (shea)share
ジェjeジェット (jetto)jet
チェcheチェック (chekku)check

sections.title: Easy to mix up
sections.html:
さ and ち

  • Both have a bar on top and a curved shape below, so they trip up almost every beginner.
  • Picture さ as a samurai holding a sword, and ち as a number 5.
  • Check the sound in a word you know: さかな (sakana, fish) starts with さ, and ちかく (chikaku, nearby) starts with ち.

し and つ

  • し is tall and hooks upward at the bottom, like a fishing hook.
  • つ is wide and flat on top, curving over and down on the right, like a wave.
  • し is shi and つ is tsu. Check yourself with すし (sushi) and つくえ (tsukue, desk).

ぬ and め

  • Both have a crossing stroke and a curl at the bottom right. ぬ ends in a loop, like the end of a noodle, and め ends in a point.
  • Check yourself with いぬ (inu, dog) and めがね (megane, eyeglasses).

ね, れ and わ

  • All three share the same tall stroke on the left, so look at the tail at the bottom right.
  • ね ends in a loop. れ ends in a kick that flicks out to the right. わ ends in a smooth, rounded curve with no loop and no flick.
  • れ is ね with the loop taken out.
  • Check yourself with ねこ (neko, cat), れいぞうこ (reizouko, refrigerator) and わたし (watashi, I).

は and ほ

  • ほ is は with one more bar. Count the bars on the right side: は has one and ほ has two.
  • Check yourself with はる (haru, spring) and ほん (hon, book).

る, ろ and ら

  • る ends in a small loop at the bottom right. ろ has no loop and ends in an open curve.
  • ら starts with a small tick on top, and the curve below it has no loop at all.
  • Check yourself with くるま (kuruma, car), ろく (roku, six) and らいげつ (raigetsu, next month).

あ and お

  • お has a small dot at the top right. あ has no dot.
  • Check yourself with あめ (ame, rain) and おかね (okane, money).

い and り

  • Both are two upright strokes. In い the left stroke is the longer one. In り the right stroke is the longer one.
  • Check yourself with いす (isu, chair) and りんご (ringo, apple).

こ and に

  • こ is just two bars. に has an upright stroke on the left in front of its two bars.
  • Check yourself with こども (kodomo, child) and にほん (nihon, Japan).

ば and ぱ: two dashes or a small circle

  • Two small dashes (dakuten) make a voiced sound, so は (ha) becomes ば (ba).
  • A small circle (handakuten) makes a p sound, so は (ha) becomes ぱ (pa).
  • The small circle is used only on the h row. The two dashes go on the k, s, t and h rows.
  • Check yourself with ばんごう (bangou, number) and かんぱい (kanpai, cheers).

じ and ぢ, ず and づ

  • ぢ sounds exactly like じ, and づ sounds exactly like ず. Romaji spells them ji and zu.
  • When you write ji or zu yourself, use じ and ず. ぢ and づ appear in only a few words, such as はなぢ (hanaji, nosebleed) and つづく (tsuzuku, to continue).
  • They show up when ち or つ becomes voiced inside a word.

お and を

  • Both are read o.
  • お is part of words, as in おかね (okane, money).
  • を is used only as a particle that marks what a verb acts on, as in ほんを よみます (hon o yomimasu, I read a book).

は, へ and を as particles

  • は is read wa, へ is read e and を is read o, but only when they work as particles.
  • Inside a word they keep their normal sounds: はる is haru and へや is heya.
  • The greetings こんにちは (konnichiwa) and こんばんは (konbanwa) end in は read wa.

Big and small kana: つ and っ, や and ゃ

  • A full-size つ says tsu. A small っ is a pause that doubles the next sound: きつね (kitsune, fox) has a full-size つ, and きって (kitte, postal stamp) has a small っ.
  • A small ゃ, ゅ or ょ blends with the kana before it into one beat. A full-size や, ゆ or よ makes a separate beat.
  • びょういん (byouin, hospital) and びよういん (biyouin, beauty salon) differ only in the size of one kana.
  • Write the small kana smaller and low on the line.

Short and long vowels

  • Length changes the word, so count the beats by tapping your finger.
  • おばさん (obasan, aunt) and おばあさん (obaasan, grandmother).
  • おじさん (ojisan, uncle) and おじいさん (ojiisan, grandfather).
  • ここ (koko, here) and こうこう (koukou, high school).
  • ゆき (yuki, snow) and ゆうき (yuuki, courage).
  • ビル (biru, building) and ビール (bi-ru, beer).
  • スパ (supa, spa) and スーパー (su-pa-, supermarket).
  • Leaving the dash out is one of the most common katakana mistakes.

ん before a vowel or y

  • ん is its own beat, so きんえん (kin'en, no smoking) has four beats and きねん (kinen, anniversary) has three.
  • Romaji shows the break with an apostrophe: kin'en and hon'ya (ほんや, bookstore).
  • Without the apostrophe, kin'en would look just like kinen, which is a different word.

Hiragana and katakana twins

  • A few characters look almost the same in both scripts: へ and ヘ, り and リ, か and カ.
  • Hiragana is round and flowing. Katakana is angular, with sharp, straight strokes.
  • When a shape is unclear, look at the words around it. A word made of other hiragana is hiragana, and a foreign word like コーヒー is katakana.
  • When a shape is unclear, look at the words around it. A foreign word like コーヒー is katakana, and a word with a Japanese ending like ます is hiragana.

シ and ツ

  • シ has two dots lying sideways and a long stroke that sweeps up from the bottom left, like a smile.
  • ツ has two dots standing upright and a long stroke that falls down to the left.
  • シ is shi and ツ is tsu. Check yourself with シンガポール (shingapo-ru, Singapore) and ツアー (tsua-, tour).

ソ and ン

  • ソ has a long stroke that starts at the top and falls down to the left, with a short stroke above it.
  • ン has a long stroke that starts low and sweeps up to the right, with a short stroke before it.
  • ソ is so and ン is n. Check yourself with ソース (so-su, sauce) and ラーメン (ra-men, ramen).

シ, ツ, ソ, ン and ミ

  • Four of these look alike at first glance. Look at the direction of the long stroke: it sweeps up in シ and ン, and it falls down in ツ and ソ.
  • Then look at the short strokes: シ and ツ have two dots, and ソ and ン have one.
  • ミ is different because it has three separate slanted lines, like the number 3.

ク and タ

  • タ is ク with one extra stroke inside it.
  • ク is ku and タ is ta. Check yourself with クラス (kurasu, class) and タクシー (takushi-, taxi).

ウ and ワ

  • ウ has a small tick on top, like a hat. ワ has no tick.
  • ウ is u and ワ is wa. Check yourself with ウール (u-ru, wool) and ワイン (wain, wine).

コ and ユ

  • コ is an open box, like a corner, with nothing sticking out.
  • ユ has a bottom line that sticks out past the box on the right.
  • コ is ko and ユ is yu. Check yourself with コーヒー (ko-hi-, coffee) and ユニフォーム (yunifo-mu, uniform).

ノ and メ

  • ノ is a single slash. メ is a slash crossed by a second stroke, like an X.
  • ノ is no and メ is me. Check yourself with ノート (no-to, notebook) and メモ (memo, memo).

バ and パ, ベ and ペ: two dashes or a small circle

  • Two small dashes (dakuten) make a voiced sound, so ハ (ha) becomes バ (ba) and ヘ (he) becomes ベ (be).
  • A small circle (handakuten) makes a p sound, so ハ (ha) becomes パ (pa) and ヘ (he) becomes ペ (pe).
  • The small circle is used only on the h row. The two dashes go on the k, s, t and h rows.
  • Check yourself with バス (basu, bus) and パン (pan, bread), and with ベッド (beddo, bed) and ペン (pen, pen).

ジ and ヂ, ズ and ヅ

  • ヂ sounds exactly like ジ, and ヅ sounds exactly like ズ. Romaji spells them ji and zu.
  • They are almost never used in katakana. When you write ji or zu yourself, use ジ and ズ.

オ and ヲ

  • Both are read o. ヲ is very rare, and you will mostly see it in the spelling ヲタク (otaku).
  • When you write o in katakana, use オ, as in オフィス (ofisu, office).

Big and small kana: ツ and ッ, ヤ and ャ

  • A full-size ツ says tsu. A small ッ is a pause that doubles the next sound: ツアー (tsua-, tour) has a full-size ツ, and カップ (kappu, cup) has a small ッ.
  • A small ャ, ュ or ョ blends with the kana before it into one beat. A full-size ヤ, ユ or ヨ makes a separate beat.
  • Write the small kana smaller and low on the line.

The long vowel mark ー and the kanji 一

  • ー is the long vowel mark. It means hold the vowel before it for twice as long, and romaji writes it as a hyphen.
  • 一 is the kanji for one (ichi). It looks like ー but it is a different character, so use the surrounding text to decide.
  • If the line comes right after a katakana letter, it is almost always the long vowel mark.

Small ァ ィ ゥ ェ ォ and full-size ア イ ウ エ オ

  • A small vowel after a full-size kana blends into one beat. ティ is ti, with one beat.
  • A full-size イ after テ makes two beats. テイ would be te-i.
  • So パーティー (pa-ti-, party) uses a small ィ, and it has four beats, not five.
  • ファイル (fairu, file) starts with ファ, which is one beat, and it is not フアイル.

ヴ and ブ

  • ヴ is ウ with two dots and stands for the English v. ブ is bu.
  • Many words that could use ヴ use バ, ビ, ブ, ベ or ボ instead, so ヴァイオリン and バイオリン are the same word.

Katakana that look like kanji

  • In a mixed text, a few katakana look almost the same as kanji. Context tells you which one it is.
  • If the character sits inside a word made of katakana, it is katakana.
  • カ (ka) and 力 (chikara, power).
  • ロ (ro) and 口 (kuchi, mouth).
  • エ (e) and 工 (kou, craft or work).
  • ニ (ni) and 二 (ni, two).
  • ハ (ha) and 八 (hachi, eight).
  • タ (ta) and 夕 (yuu, evening).
  • ミ (mi) and 三 (san, three).
